description: Hi I'm Naim from Argentina, with skills in design. I'll be taking on The Earth Information Jukebox challenge.
summary: Earth Beats is an Earth Information Jukebox: a web page where you pick a NASA Earth visualization and hear it. The page reads the colors of every video frame and turns them into sound in real time. Lightning detected from the International Space Station becomes real thunder, city lights at night become high, star-like bells, and sea temperature becomes a river that runs faster and higher as the water gets warmer. Each visualization is wrapped on a 3D globe you can turn. It is designed for blind and low-vision people: it is built to work with a keyboard and a screen reader, it describes in text what is sounding, and a "Sound key" lets you hear each sound on its own before listening to the whole planet. NASA's Earth visualizations are silent; Earth Beats lets people who can't see them listen to the same data.
details:
WHAT IT DOES. Earth Beats has three tracks, each one a NASA visualization: Lightning from space, Night lights and Ocean temperature. Tap a track to play it and tap it again to pause. While it plays, you hear the data.

HOW IT WORKS. Ten times per second the page takes the current video frame, shrinks it to 96x54 pixels and counts colors. Lightning: yellow pixels that were not in the previous frame are new flashes; each one triggers a real thunder recording, panned to the side where it appears, and many flashes at once bring in storm rain. Night lights: bright pixels become high bells (more light, more bells) and darkness is a low drone; in the change map, violet (more light than in 2012) plays a major chord and orange (less light) a minor chord. Ocean temperature: the hue from blue to red is read as cold to warm; cold water is a slow, distant river with a low chord, warm water is a fast, close river pitched higher the warmer it is, and the movement of the currents changes its volume.

ACCESSIBILITY. Everything works with a keyboard. The page is built so that screen readers announce the track, its state, a description of the video and what is sounding (this can be turned off so it doesn't talk over the sound). The Sound key pairs each color with its sound and a "Hear" button. Text contrast meets WCAG AA, touch targets are at least 44 px, and the globe stops spinning for people who ask for reduced motion. It has not been tested with blind users yet.

WHAT I HOPE TO ACHIEVE. I want blind kids to see the Earth with their ears. Next steps: test it with blind and low-vision users, add more visualizations from the Earth Information Center, and bring it to science classes and museums.

TOOLS. HTML, CSS and JavaScript; Web Audio API; three.js; ffmpeg; Cloudflare Workers (hosting).

USE OF AI. I used Claude Code (Anthropic), an AI coding assistant. The idea is mine: letting blind kids hear NASA's Earth visualizations. The AI wrote all the code of the website following my decisions and corrections (acknowledged in the page footer and in the source files), ran a usability and accessibility review, and proposed options for sounds and for the video script, from which I chose. The thunder, rain and river sounds are real CC0 recordings, not AI-generated; the bells, chords and drones are synthesized in the browser by that AI-written code. In the demo video, the motion graphics and the editing were made with AI assistance and carry a visible "AI-assisted graphics" watermark; the AI also helped me word the script in English, cleaned the audio of my recordings and softened the on-camera image. The voice and the on-camera footage are mine. The screen recordings show the real website in an earlier build (it still had a playback bar that I later removed). No AI-generated images, voices or music were used. No NASA logos or branding were used.

SPANISH VERSION of the demo video (English subtitles): https://youtu.be/dMIBTqQ2-PM
